claim: Co-infected hosts have been suggested to facilitate pathogen transmission, including the emergence of supershedding events.
source: Co-infected hosts, individuals that carry more than one infectious agent at any one time, have been suggested to facilitate pathogen transmission, including the emergence of supershedding events.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references existing literature suggesting a relationship between co-infection and transmission dynamics.

claim: Rabbits co-infected with one or both helminths shed significantly more B. bronchiseptica than rabbits with bacteria alone.
source: Experimental data showed that rabbits co-infected with one or both helminths shed significantly more B. bronchiseptica, by direct contact with an agar petri dish, than rabbits with bacteria alone.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements comparing shedding levels between infection groups.

claim: Co-infected hosts generated supershedding events of higher intensity and more frequently than hosts with no helminths.
source: Co-infected hosts generated supershedding events of higher intensity and more frequently than hosts with no helminths.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and quantitative analysis of shedding events.

claim: Differences in the magnitude and duration of shedding could be explained by the effect of the two helminths on the relative contribution of neutrophils and specific IgA and IgG to B. bronchiseptica neutralization in the respiratory tract.
source: Simulations suggested that differences in the magnitude and duration of shedding could be explained by the effect of the two helminths on the relative contribution of neutrophils and specific IgA and IgG to B. bronchiseptica neutralization in the respiratory tract.
evidence: This claim is based on computational model simulations fitted to experimental data.

claim: The interactions between infection and immune response at the scale of analysis used could not capture the rapid variation in the intensity of shedding of every rabbit.
source: However, the interactions between infection and immune response at the scale of analysis that we used could not capture the rapid variation in the intensity of shedding of every rabbit.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on their modeling results compared to observed data.

claim: Fast and local changes at the level of respiratory tissue probably played a more important role in rapid shedding variation.
source: We suggest that fast and local changes at the level of respiratory tissue probably played a more important role.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation by the authors to explain patterns not captured by their model.

claim: Individual variation in pathogen transmission can increase the basic reproduction number R0 of a pathogen.
source: Individual variation in pathogen transmission can increase the basic reproduction number R0 of a pathogen and determine whether an infection will invade and spread or stutter and quickly fade out in a population of susceptible hosts (Keeling et al., 2001; Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Some infected hosts shed disproportionately more and for longer than the average population, called supershedders.
source: One of the causes of this variation is associated with differences in the amount and duration of pathogen shedding, whereby some infected hosts shed disproportionately more and for longer than the average population, the so called supershedders (Chase-Topping et al., 2008; Gopinath et al., 2013), while others do not shed at all (Chen et al., 2006; Hadinoto et al., 2009; Leung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a definition supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: B. bronchiseptica is a highly contagious bacterium of the respiratory tract that infects a wide range of mammals.
source: B. bronchiseptica is a highly contagious bacterium of the respiratory tract that causes multiple symptoms and infects a wide range of mammals (Goodnow, 1980).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pathogen, supported by citation.

claim: B. bronchiseptica is removed from the lower respiratory tract via phagocytosis stimulated by a Th1 inflammatory reaction involving cell mediated antibodies and neutrophils.
source: In rabbits and mice, and likely other mammal species, B. bronchiseptica is removed from the lower respiratory tract (lungs and trachea) via phagocytosis stimulated by a Th1 inflammatory reaction that involves cell mediated antibodies and neutrophils (Thakar et al., 2007; Thakar et al., 2009; Thakar et al., 2012).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Bacteria persist in the nasal cavity, although they are partially reduced by IgA antibodies in naïve and immunized mice.
source: Bacteria persist in the nasal cavity, although they are partially reduced by IgA antibodies in naïve and immunized mice (Kirimanjeswara et al., 2003; Wolfe et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work in mice.

claim: Transmission is poor among wild-type laboratory mice but increases among TLR4-deficient mice.
source: Transmission is poor among wild-type laboratory mice but increases among TLR4-deficient mice (Rolin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: The intensity of shedding has been found to be positively correlated with neutrophil counts in TLR4-deficient mice.
source: The TLR4-deficient response is associated with neutrophil infiltration, and the intensity of shedding has been found to be positively correlated with neutrophil counts.
evidence: This is based on findings from the cited study on TLR4-deficient mice.

claim: Rabbits naturally shed and efficiently transmit B. bronchiseptica between animals.
source: In contrast, rabbits naturally shed (Pathak et al., 2010) and efficiently transmit B. bronchiseptica between animals (Long et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: B. bronchiseptica spills-over into humans but there is no evidence of sustained onward transmission.
source: Occasionally, B. bronchiseptica spills-over into humans but there is no evidence of sustained onward transmission, as these human infections have invariably occurred in immunocompromised individuals (Goodnow, 1980; Woolfrey and Moody, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical observations.

claim: Humans are primarily infected by the species B. pertussis and B. parapertussis which are responsible for regular whooping cough outbreaks worldwide.
source: Humans are primarily infected by the species B. pertussis and B. parapertussis which are responsible for regular whooping cough outbreaks worldwide (Domenech de Cellès et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human Bordetella infections, supported by citation.

claim: B. bronchiseptica provides a good model system to explore the dynamics of shedding in Bordetella infections and the interaction with other infectious agents.
source: Given the close relatedness between Bordetella species, and considering the many similarities in the kinetics of infection and the immune response, B. bronchiseptica provides a good model system to explore the dynamics of shedding in Bordetella infections and the interaction with other infectious agents, like gastrointestinal helminths.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarities between Bordetella species.

claim: B. bronchiseptica contributes to exacerbate respiratory symptoms in co-infections with other respiratory pathogens, including the development of acute pulmonary disease and bronchopneumonia.
source: In co-infections with other respiratory pathogens B. bronchiseptica contributes to exacerbate respiratory symptoms, including the development of acute pulmonary disease and bronchopneumonia, and ultimately host death (Brockmeier et al., 2008; Loving et al., 2010; Schulz et al., 2014; Kureljušić et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Parasitic helminths commonly stimulate a Th2 anti-inflammatory immune response that interferes with the Th1 response developed against B. bronchiseptica.
source: Parasitic helminths commonly stimulate a Th2 anti-inflammatory immune response that interferes with the Th1 response developed against B. bronchiseptica and related species (Brady et al., 1999; Pathak et al., 2012; Thakar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous immunological studies.

claim: Rabbits co-infected with either T. retortaeformis or G. strigosum carried higher B. bronchiseptica infections in the nasal cavity but there were no significant differences in the size and duration of infection in the lungs, when compared to rabbits infected with bacteria alone.
source: We recently showed that rabbits co-infected with either T. retortaeformis or G. strigosum carried higher B. bronchiseptica infections in the nasal cavity but there were no significant differences in the size and duration of infection in the lungs, when compared to rabbits infected with bacteria alone (Pathak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2012; Thakar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on previous experimental work by the authors.

claim: T. retortaeformis is reduced or cleared from the small intestine while G. strigosum persists with high intensities in the stomach.
source: These two helminths stimulate a similar immune response, however, while the former is reduced or cleared from the small intestine, the latter persists with high intensities in the stomach (Cattadori et al., 2005; Cattadori et al., 2008; Cattadori et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Neutrophils and antibodies IgA and IgG are important to bacterial clearance from the lungs.
source: The modeling of the immune network in B. bronchiseptica-T. retortaeformis rabbits and B. bronchiseptica alone animals suggested that neutrophils and antibodies IgA and IgG are important to bacterial clearance from the lungs (Thakar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on previous modeling work cited.

claim: There was large variation in the level at which B. bronchiseptica was shed both within and between the four types of infection.
source: There was large variation in the level at which B. bronchiseptica was shed both within and between the four types of infection (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: 3 out of 16 B. bronchiseptica only animals did not shed at all.
source: Some rabbits consistently shed large amounts of CFUs while others were low shedders or did not shed at all, specifically: 3 out of 16 for B. bronchiseptica only animals (B), 1 out of 23 for B. bronchiseptica-G. strigosum (BG), 3 out of 20 for B. bronchiseptica-T. retortaeformis (BT) and 0 out of 24 for the triple infection (BTG).
evidence: This is a direct count from experimental observations.

claim: High shedders were found during the first 60 days post infection.
source: High shedders were found during the first 60 days post infection, although some of these rabbits continued to shed a large number of bacteria well beyond this time (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The level of shedding was significantly higher in rabbits co-infected with helminths than B. bronchiseptica only animals (BTG: 0.42, 0.31–0.54; BG: 0.32, 0.25–0.41; BT: 0.26, 0.18–0.35 and B: 0.02,–0.01-0.03; p<0.05).
source: The level of shedding was significantly higher in rabbits co-infected with helminths than B. bronchiseptica only animals (mean shedding (CFU/s) and 95% CI, BTG: 0.42, 0.31–0.54; BG: 0.32, 0.25–0.41; BT: 0.26, 0.18–0.35 and B: 0.02,–0.01-0.03; Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni correction for multiple testing, for all: p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: No significant differences in shedding were observed among the three co-infected groups.
source: When we considered the co-infected hosts, no significant differences were observed among the three groups (p>0.05) although the triple infection showed a tendency for higher shedding (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Up to 55% of the shedding events were classified as null, where rabbits interacted with the petri dish but did not shed even though they were known to be infected.
source: Across the four infections up to 55% of the shedding events were classified as null, where rabbits interacted with the petri dish but did not shed even though they were known to be infected (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The highest percentage of null shedding was found in the B. bronchiseptica only group (56.2%).
source: The highest percentage was found in the B. bronchiseptica only group (56.2%), followed by the dual infections (BT: 40.3% and BG: 29.8%) and last the triple infection BTG (25.8%) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct calculation from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The BTG group showed the largest variation in the level of shedding (Negative Binomial k=0.21, 0.16–0.26).
source: This latter group showed the largest variation in the level of shedding (Negative Binomial k and 95% CI, BTG: 0.21, 0.16–0.26) followed by the dual infections BG (0.37, 0.29–0.45) and BT (0.45, 0.33–0.57); for all, the distribution was not significantly different from the frequency data (p>0.05).
evidence: This is based on statistical modeling of the experimental data.

claim: The presence of helminths increased the level of bacteria shed in the environment and the frequency of these events.
source: These findings suggest that the presence of helminths increased the level of bacteria shed in the environment and the frequency of these events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Having helminths increased the variation in the magnitude of shedding events among rabbits within the same group as well as between groups.
source: Having helminths also increased the variation in the magnitude of these events among rabbits within the same group as well as between groups.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Co-infections with helminths should lead to a higher probability of B. bronchiseptica onward transmission given a contact.
source: Together these findings indicate that co-infections with helminths, irrespective of the species, should lead to a higher probability of B. bronchiseptica onward transmission given a contact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in shedding levels.

claim: Using the 99th percentile threshold of CFU/s=0.27 from B. bronchiseptica only rabbits, none of the B rabbits can be classified as supershedders.
source: If we estimate this threshold using B. bronchiseptica only infected animals, and define supershedders as the hosts that have at least one shedding event above this threshold, for example the 99th percentile, our cut-off value is CFU/s=0.27 (Figure 3). This indicates that none of the rabbits with B. bronchiseptica (0 out of 13) can be classified as supershedders.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Using the 99th percentile threshold from B only rabbits, 59% of BG, 53% of BT, and 42% of BTG rabbits are supershedders.
source: However, if we apply the same cut-off to the co-infected groups the percentage is considerably high, namely: 59% (13 out of 22) for BG, 53% (9 out of 17) for BT and 42% (10 out of 24) for the BTG group.
evidence: This is based on applying the threshold to experimental data.

claim: Using the 99th percentile threshold from the whole dataset (CFU/s=8.58), 0% of B, 32% of BG, 18% of BT, and 21% of BTG rabbits had at least one supershedding event.
source: When we apply this approach the 99th percentile threshold is now CFU/s=8.58 and the fraction of hosts with, at least, one supershedding event above this value is: 0% (0 out of 13) for B, 32% (7 out of 22) for BG, 18% (3 out of 17) BT and 21% (5 out of 24) for BTG (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the entire experimental dataset.

claim: Using the 95th percentile threshold from the whole dataset (CFU/s=2.71), the number of rabbits with at least one supershedding event is 0% for B, 45% for BG, 29% for BT, and 29% for BTG.
source: Similarly, if we select the less limiting 95th percentile threshold, the new common value decreases to CFU/s=2.71 and the number of rabbits with at least one supershedding event is still zero for B but increases to 45% (10 out of 22) for BG, 29% (5 out of 17) for BT and 29% (7 out of 24) for BTG (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the entire experimental dataset.

claim: Supershedding events were found more often in the initial four/five weeks post infection.
source: Consistent with the general pattern of shedding, supershedding events were found more often in the initial four/five weeks post infection (Figures 1 and 2), although later events were also observed, especially for the BG and BTG groups, and with some rabbits contributing multiple times.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: There was a rapid bacterial replication following the initial inoculum.
source: Consistently among the four types of infection, simulations indicated that there was a rapid bacterial replication following the initial inoculum, the growth rate, r, was high for BTG (group level value and [95% CI]: 1.47 [1.10–1.83]) and BG (1.18 [0.83–1.54]), less so for BT (1.01 [0.83–1.18]) and much lower for B single infection (0.06 [0.006–0.12]) (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on model simulations fitted to experimental data.

claim: Model fitting well captured the empirical trends of neutrophils and specific antibodies over time.
source: Model fitting well captured the empirical trends of neutrophils and specific antibodies over time, both as a profile representative of each type of infection and as a trend of every rabbit within each group (Table 2, Figure 5).
evidence: This is an assessment of model performance against experimental data.

claim: In all four groups, neutrophils showed the fastest rate of increase, followed by specific IgA and then specific IgG.
source: In all four groups, neutrophils showed the fastest rate of increase, a1, with a tendency to be faster in B. bronchiseptica only rabbits, followed by specific IgA and then specific IgG (Table 2, Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates from experimental data.

claim: Neutrophils were the fastest to decrease and to return to original values with the neutralization of bacteria from the respiratory tract.
source: Neutrophils were also the fastest to decrease, at a rate b1, and to return to original values with the neutralization, albeit no complete clearance, of bacteria from the respiratory tract (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is based on model simulations and experimental observations.

claim: B. bronchiseptica is removed from lungs and trachea but persists in the nasal cavity.
source: As reported in our previous studies of this system, B. bronchiseptica is removed from lungs and trachea but persists in the nasal cavity (Pathak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2012; Thakar et al., 2012), a pattern also observed in mice (Kirimanjeswara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: IgG reached the asymptotic value at around 20 days post infection and remained high throughout the trials.
source: The increase of specific IgA and IgG was slow, however, once IgG reached the asymptotic value at around 20 days post infection, it remained high throughout the trials, while IgA peaked around day 20 and slowly decreased thereafter, although it had not fallen to baseline levels by the end of the trials (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and model simulations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The relative contribution of neutrophils, IgA, and IgG to B. bronchiseptica neutralization varied among the four types of infection.
source: The relative contribution of the three immune variables to B. bronchiseptica neutralization, c1, c2, c3, varied among the four types of infection.
evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates from experimental data.

claim: Neutrophils primarily controlled bacteria in the single infection.
source: Model fittings suggested that neutrophils primarily controlled bacteria in the single infection, whereas a combination of neutrophils and specific IgG were probably important in BTG rabbits (Table 2, Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates and simulations.

claim: A combination of neutrophils and specific IgG were probably important in BTG rabbits.
source: Model fittings suggested that neutrophils primarily controlled bacteria in the single infection, whereas a combination of neutrophils and specific IgG were probably important in BTG rabbits (Table 2, Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates and simulations.

claim: The coupling of IgG and IgA could contribute to explain the neutralization of bacteria in the BT group.
source: The coupling of IgG and IgA could contribute to explain the neutralization of bacteria in the BT group while neutrophils and IgG appeared to be relevant in the BG group.
evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates and simulations.

claim: Neutrophils and IgG appeared to be relevant in the BG group.
source: The coupling of IgG and IgA could contribute to explain the neutralization of bacteria in the BT group while neutrophils and IgG appeared to be relevant in the BG group.
evidence: This is based on model parameter estimates and simulations.

claim: Neutrophils are expected to primarily control B. bronchiseptica early on in the infection.
source: Given the early reaction of neutrophils, they are expected to primarily control B. bronchiseptica early on in the infection, while specific IgG and, secondly, specific IgA appear to be more important at a later time, as they decreased more slowly, such is the case for IgA, or remained consistently high over the course of the infection, like for IgG (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics observed in the data and model.

claim: Specific IgG and IgA appear to be more important at a later time in controlling B. bronchiseptica.
source: Given the early reaction of neutrophils, they are expected to primarily control B. bronchiseptica early on in the infection, while specific IgG and, secondly, specific IgA appear to be more important at a later time, as they decreased more slowly, such is the case for IgA, or remained consistently high over the course of the infection, like for IgG (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics observed in the data and model.

claim: The immune response changed both between individuals within a group and between groups.
source: An investigation of the posterior parameter estimations confirmed that the immune response changed both between individuals within a group and between groups (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of model parameter estimates.

claim: The estimated time to reach the peak of shedding was between 10 and 12 days post infection for the co-infected groups.
source: The estimated time to reach the peak of shedding was between 10 and 12 days post infection for the co-infected groups, specifically: 9 days for BTG, 11 days for BT and 12 days for BG.
evidence: This is based on model simulations fitted to experimental data.

claim: The peak value of shedding was 14,185 CFU/day (11.06–12,258,022) for BTG, 8,266 (5.89–10,119,754) for BG, and 7,863 (29.57–2,213,310) for BT.
source: For example, the peak value (CFU/day; 95% CIs) was: 14,185 (11.06–12,258,022) for BTG, 8,266 (5.89–10,119,754) for BG and 7,863 (29.57–2,213,310) for BT.
evidence: This is based on model simulations fitted to experimental data.

claim: Rabbits from the BTG infection exhibited the most rapid increase of shedding, the highest levels and the slowest decline post-peak.
source: Rabbits from the BTG infection exhibited the most rapid increase of shedding, the highest levels and the slowest decline post-peak, suggesting a possible synergistic effect of the two helminths.
evidence: This is based on model simulations and experimental observations.

claim: The two helminths in the BTG infection may have a synergistic effect.
source: Rabbits from the BTG infection exhibited the most rapid increase of shedding, the highest levels and the slowest decline post-peak, suggesting a possible synergistic effect of the two helminths.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observed patterns.

claim: The BT group showed the most rapid decline in shedding.
source: The BT group showed the most rapid decline, while rabbits from the BG group maintained a trend intermediate between the BTG and BT groups (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on model simulations and experimental observations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Rabbits showed rapid changes in the level of shedding between consecutive samplings, where bursts of bacteria alternated to low or no shedding in a matter of a few days.
source: Rabbits showed rapid changes in the level of shedding between consecutive samplings, where bursts of bacteria alternated to low or no shedding in a matter of a few days.
evidence: This is a direct observation from experimental data.

claim: This rapid dynamic could not be explained by the intensity of infection and related immune responses at the scale used to record such data.
source: This rapid dynamic could not be explained by the intensity of infection and related immune responses at the scale used to record such data.
evidence: This is an assessment of model limitations based on comparison with data.

claim: Changes in local conditions, such as variation in the severity of tissue inflammation or control of bacteria at the mucosa level, had a stronger impact on fast changes in shedding.
source: Instead, it is possible that changes in local conditions, such as variation in the severity of tissue inflammation or control of bacteria at the mucosa level, including changes in the amount of mucus formation and expulsion, had a stronger impact on these fast changes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for patterns not captured by the model.

claim: Co-infected rabbits sniffled more frequently than B. bronchiseptica only animals.
source: We also noted that co-infected rabbits sniffled more frequently than B. bronchiseptica only animals (Pathak's pers. obs.) and, probably, further contributed to alter the frequency and intensity of these events.
evidence: This is based on personal observation during experiments.

claim: An increase in the rate of bacterial neutralization led to a proportional decrease of the peak of shedding and the time to reach this peak.
source: Findings showed that an increase in the rate of bacterial neutralization, μc , and, secondly, in the mmune growth rate, μa, led to a proportional decrease of the peak of shedding and, to a lesser extent, the time to reach this peak (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the model.

claim: The strongest negative impact on shedding was caused by changes in neutrophil and IgG rates.
source: Among the three immune variables, the strongest negative impact on shedding was caused by changes in neutrophil (c1 or a1) and IgG (c3 or a3) rates.
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the model.

claim: An increase in bacterial growth rate was associated with a higher peak of shedding and a shorter time to reach this peak.
source: As expected, an increase in bacterial growth rate, r, was associated with a higher peak of shedding and, consequently, a shorter time to reach this peak (Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the model.

claim: The three co-infections exhibited comparable trends and were more sensitive to immune changes than B. bronchiseptica only infected rabbits.
source: Overall, the three co-infections exhibited comparable trends and were more sensitive to immune changes than B. bronchiseptica only infected rabbits.
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis of the model.

claim: The weak response of the B group was probably caused by the very low bacterial growth rate (r=0.06) and thus shedding, suggesting a stronger immune control.
source: The weak response of the latter group was probably caused by the very low bacterial growth rate (r=0.06) and thus shedding, suggesting a stronger immune control.
evidence: This is an inference based on model parameter estimates.

claim: Gastrointestinal helminths can impact the severity and time course of respiratory bacterial infections.
source: There is increasing evidence that gastrointestinal helminths can impact the severity and time course of respiratory bacterial infections (Brady et al., 1999; Lass et al., 2013; Diniz et al., 2010; Ezenwa et al., 2010; Babu and Nutman, 2016; Long et al., 2019); however, how they affect the dynamics of shedding remains to be determined.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The two helminths significantly increased the level, the variation and the duration of shedding, along with enhancing the frequency of supershedding events.
source: Empirical findings showed that the two helminths, taken as a single species or as a pair, significantly increased the level, the variation and the duration of shedding, along with enhancing the frequency of supershedding events.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: These changes in shedding were related to the significant growth of bacteria in the respiratory tract.
source: Model estimates suggested that these changes were related to the significant growth of bacteria in the respiratory tract.
evidence: This is based on model simulations.

claim: The development of an immune response controlled the infection and led to the waning but not the complete clearance of B. bronchiseptica.
source: The developed of an immune response controlled the infection and led to the waning but not the complete clearance of B. bronchiseptica.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and model simulations.

claim: The decline of shedding in the first 90 days post infection could be explained by the immune-mediated clearance of B. bronchiseptica from the lungs.
source: The decline of shedding in the first 90 days post infection could be explained by the immune-mediated clearance of B. bronchiseptica from the lungs, previously reported using data from these experiments (Pathak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2012; Thakar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on model simulations and previous experimental findings.

claim: The reduced but ongoing shedding later in the experiments could be the result of the weak control of bacteria in the nasal cavity.
source: In contrast, the reduced but ongoing shedding later in the experiments could be the result of the weak control of bacteria in the nasal cavity (Pathak et al., 2010; Pathak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on model simulations and previous experimental findings.

claim: The two helminth species appeared not to change the general trend of immune variables but the timing and intensity of their relative contribution.
source: We found that neutrophils quickly increased and contributed to bacteria neutralization early on, these were then followed by antibodies that developed more slowly and with an initial delay in the co-infected hosts. The two helminth species appeared not to change the general trend of these variables but the timing and intensity of their relative contribution and, with this, temporal changes in the level of shedding.
evidence: This is based on model simulations and experimental observations.

claim: Both T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum elicit a Th-2 immune response.
source: We previously showed that both helminths elicit a Th-2 immune response (Murphy et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2013; Cattadori et al., 2019), however, while T. retortaeformis was cleared, or significantly reduced from the small intestine, G. strigosum persisted with high intensities in the stomach (Cattadori et al., 2005; Cattadori et al., 2008; Cattadori et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2013; Mignatti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The faster decline of shedding in BT rabbits could have been caused by the stronger immune control of B. bronchiseptica, probably facilitated by the rapid clearance of T. retortaeformis.
source: It is conceivable to think that the faster decline of shedding in rabbits from the BT than the BG or BTG group could have been caused by the stronger immune control of B. bronchiseptica, probably facilitated by the rapid clearance of T. retortaeformis (Thakar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observed patterns and previous findings.

claim: The persistence of G. strigosum in the stomach probably contributed to delay the decline of shedding and to increase the magnitude of these events.
source: In contrast, the persistence of G. strigosum in the stomach probably contributed to delay the decline of shedding and to increase the magnitude of these events, including increasing the frequency of supershedding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observed patterns.

claim: In the BTG triple infection the two helminths appeared to have a positive synergistic effect particularly in delaying the decline of shedding.
source: Interestingly, in the BTG triple infection the two helminths appeared to have a positive synergistic effect particularly in delaying the decline of shedding.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed patterns in the data.

claim: T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum are commonly found in populations of rabbits.
source: Given these patterns, and considering that T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum are commonly found in populations of rabbits, it is not surprising if these helminths play an important role to the rapid transmission and persistence of B. bronchiseptica in natural settings.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of natural rabbit populations.

claim: The annual prevalence of B. bronchiseptica in a free-living population of rabbits ranged between 88% and 97%.
source: For example, the serological study of a free-living population of rabbits showed that the annual prevalence of B. bronchiseptica ranged between 88% and 97% (Pathak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous field study.

claim: 65% of rabbits in a free-living population were co-infected with B. bronchiseptica and G. strigosum.
source: Of these rabbits 65% were co-infected with B. bronchiseptica and G. strigosum, and both bacterial prevalence and helminth intensity increased with rabbit age.
evidence: This is based on data from a previous field study.

claim: About 60% of adult rabbits in a free-living population carried BTG infections.
source: Although the study did not examine these patterns in dual or triple infections with T. retortaeformis, about 60% of adult rabbits were found to carry BTG infections (unpubl. data), suggesting that rabbits co-infected with helminths represent a large fraction of this host population and, together with the dual infections, are probably responsible for the high prevalence of B. bronchiseptica throughout the years.
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from field observations.

claim: The combined effect of antigen-antibody complex and phagocytosis, activated by neutrophils, were important for bacterial removal from the lungs.
source: Recent Boolean modeling of the whole immune network to B. bronchiseptica infection indicated that the combined effect of antigen-antibody complex and phagocytosis, activated by neutrophils among others, were important for bacterial removal from the lungs (Thakar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claim: Serum antibodies cleared B. bronchiseptica from lungs and trachea of wild-type and B-cell-deficient mice within 3 days post inoculation.
source: The important role of antibodies to B. bronchiseptica control was empirically highlighted in the mouse model where serum antibodies (which include IgG isotypes and IgA) cleared B. bronchiseptica from lungs and trachea of wild-type and B-cell-deficient mice within 3 days post inoculation (Kirimanjeswara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: IgA was found to be necessary for the reduction of bacterial numbers in the nasal cavity of mice.
source: Similarly, IgA was found to be necessary for the reduction of bacterial numbers in the nasal cavity of mice (Wolfe et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: There was an early peak of neutrophils in the blood of rabbits infected with the two helminths, likely a consequence of gut bacteria infiltrating in the mucosa damaged during helminth establishment.
source: In our previous work we found an early peak of neutrophils in the blood of rabbits infected with our two helminths and suggested that this was likely a consequence of gut bacteria infiltrating in the mucosa damaged during helminth establishment in the gastrointestinal tract (Murphy et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on previous experimental observations and interpretation.

claim: Previous work found no temporal differences in bacterial clearance from the lungs of rabbits from the B and the BT groups.
source: Although we were not able to disentangle the proportion of neutrophils that were stimulated by and directed against B. bronchiseptica, previous work by Thakar et al., 2012 found no temporal differences in bacterial clearance from the lungs of rabbits from the B and the BT groups, suggesting that there is probably no significant interference from the gut-stimulated neutrophils.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Gut-restricted helminths could enhance the neutrophil response in the respiratory tract in mice co-infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Heligmosomoides polygyrus.
source: The evidence that gut-restricted helminths could enhance the neutrophil response in the respiratory tract was showed in mice co-infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the lungs and Heligmosomoides polygyrus in the gastrointestinal tract (Long et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: Survival rate was improved in mice co-infected with P. aeruginosa and H. polygyrus compared to mice with bacteria alone.
source: This study found a higher recruitment of neutrophils in the lungs together with an increase of CD4 +T cells and Th2 cytokine expression. Interestingly, survival rate was improved in co-infected mice than mice with bacteria alone, suggesting that neutrophils, rather than a Th2 response, dominated in the lungs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: TLR4-mutant mice infected with B. bronchiseptica poorly controlled bacterial growth and shedding.
source: Work by Rolin et al., 2014 showed that TLR4-mutant mice infected with B. bronchiseptica poorly controlled bacterial growth and shedding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: In TLR4-mutant mice, the depletion of neutrophils did not affect the level of infection but decreased individual shedding.
source: Animals exhibited heavy neutrophil infiltration in the lungs, however, the depletion of neutrophils did not affect the level of infection but decreased individual shedding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: The possible interference with a Th2 immune signal stimulated by T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum contributed to increase the level and duration of B. bronchiseptica shedding.
source: Taken together, we propose that the possible interference with a Th2 immune signal stimulated by T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum contributed to increase the level and duration of B. bronchiseptica shedding, although this anti-inflammatory response was not sufficiently strong to prevent bacteria clearance from the lower respiratory tract.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on integration of findings.

claim: The anti-inflammatory response was not sufficiently strong to prevent bacteria clearance from the lower respiratory tract.
source: Taken together, we propose that the possible interference with a Th2 immune signal stimulated by T. retortaeformis and G. strigosum contributed to increase the level and duration of B. bronchiseptica shedding, although this anti-inflammatory response was not sufficiently strong to prevent bacteria clearance from the lower respiratory tract.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Other processes generated the exponential bursts and timing of (super)shedding observed, including immune-mediated control of bacteria turnover in the mucosa or stochastic events during bacteria release.
source: Most likely, other processes generated the exponential bursts and timing of (super)shedding observed. These could include, but are not limited to, immune-mediated control of bacteria turnover in the mucosa or stochastic events during bacteria release, such as random mucus discharge, and also variation in host behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for patterns not captured by the model.

claim: Fast, intermittent shedding has been reported in other systems from both single and co-infected hosts.
source: Our finding is consistent with other systems where fast, intermittent shedding was reported both from single (Hadinoto et al., 2009; Schiffer et al., 2009; Rolin et al., 2014; Spencer et al., 2015; Slater et al., 2016) and co-infected hosts (Byrne et al., 2019; Kao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Epstein-Barr virus was rapidly and continuously shed in the saliva of healthy carriers, and the process of virus production and control was regulated by multiple factors, including the immune response.
source: A compelling study by Hadinoto et al., 2009 on Epstein-Barr virus shedding in healthy carriers showed that the virus was rapidly and continuously shed in the saliva but the process of virus production and control was regulated by multiple factors, including the immune response.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Variation in the level and frequency of Epstein-Barr virus shedding was a process that occurred at the individual level over time.
source: Importantly, they showed that variation in the level and frequency of shedding was a process that occurred at the individual level over time.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: This study shows variation in B. bronchiseptica shedding at three levels: between types of infection, between hosts with each infection type, and within each host over time.
source: Our study further supports this finding by showing variation in B. bronchiseptica shedding at three levels: between types of infection, between hosts with each infection type, and within each host over time.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the current study.

claim: The model framework and scale of analysis was able to describe variation between types of infection and between hosts but not within hosts over time.
source: Our model framework, and the scale of our analysis, was able to describe the first two types of variation but prevented us from capturing the local mechanism responsible for the rapid changes observed at the individual level.
evidence: This is an assessment of model capabilities and limitations.

claim: A cut-off value based on single infection can lead to the overestimation of supershedding in co-infected rabbits.
source: Our analysis showed that a cut-off value based on single infection can lead to the overestimation of supershedding in co-infected rabbits.
evidence: This is an inference based on analysis of threshold definitions.

claim: Between 18% and 32% of the co-infected rabbits generated at least one supershedding event using the 99th percentile threshold from the whole dataset.
source: We used two closely related helminth species and if we consider the 99th percentile threshold, we found that between 18% and 32% of the co-infected rabbits generated at least one supershedding event, which greatly contrast with the lack of cases from the B. bronchiseptica only rabbits.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Given the magnitude and frequency of supershedding, the risk of onwards transmission following a contact is likely to non-linearly increase for the co-infected hosts.
source: Therefore, we can speculate that given the magnitude and frequency of supershedding, the risk of onwards transmission following a contact is likely to non-linearly increase for the co-infected hosts.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on observed patterns.

claim: One quarter of the global human population is infected with helminths.
source: Given that one quarter of the global human population is infected with helminths and considering that respiratory infections are among the top 10 causes of death by infectious diseases worldwide, understanding the modulatory role of helminth species to respiratory infections is important for developing treatments targeted to specific co-infection settings.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Respiratory infections are among the top 10 causes of death by infectious diseases worldwide.
source: Given that one quarter of the global human population is infected with helminths and considering that respiratory infections are among the top 10 causes of death by infectious diseases worldwide, understanding the modulatory role of helminth species to respiratory infections is important for developing treatments targeted to specific co-infection settings.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Understanding the modulatory role of helminth species to respiratory infections is important for developing treatments targeted to specific co-infection settings.
source: Given that one quarter of the global human population is infected with helminths and considering that respiratory infections are among the top 10 causes of death by infectious diseases worldwide, understanding the modulatory role of helminth species to respiratory infections is important for developing treatments targeted to specific co-infection settings.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical implications of the research.

claim: The ability to detect and control high shedders and/or supershedders is critical for reducing the risk of disease outbreak and spread.
source: The ability to detect and, ideally, control the high shedders and/or supershedders is also critical for reducing the risk of disease outbreak and spread, and should not be overlooked any longer.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical implications of the research.

claim: B. bronchiseptica strain RB50 was used for all experiments.
source: We used B. bronchiseptica strain RB50 for all experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: Bacteria were grown on Bordet-Gengou (BG) agar supplemented with 10% defibrinated sheep blood and streptomycin (20 μg/ml).
source: Bacteria were grown on Bordet-Gengou (BG) agar supplemented with 10% defibrinated sheep blood and streptomycin (20 μg/ml).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: New Zealand White, two months old, male rabbits were used for the experiments.
source: New Zealand White, two months old, male rabbits (Harlan, USA), were challenged with B. bronchiseptica and two helminth species as follow: i- B. bronchiseptica (B) single infection: 32 infected and 16 controls, ii- B. bronchiseptica-Graphidium strigosum (BG): 31 infected and 16 controls, iii- B. bronchiseptica-T. retortaeformis (BT): 32 infected and 16 controls, and iv- the three agents together (BTG): 32 infected and 16 controls.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: For the co-infections animals received, simultaneously by gavage, a single inoculum of water (5 ml) with either 5500 T. retortaeformis or 650 G. strigosum third stage infective larvae, or both.
source: For the co-infections animals also received, simultaneously by gavage, a single inoculum of water (5 ml) with either 5500T. retortaeformis or 650 G. strigosum third stage infective larvae, or both.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: Helminth doses followed natural infections.
source: Helminth doses followed natural infections (Cattadori et al., 2005; Cattadori et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citations.

claim: The dynamics of infection and related immune responses were followed for 120 days (150 days for B) by sacrificing four infected and two control animals at fixed days post infection.
source: The dynamics of infection and related immune responses were then followed for 120 days (150 days for B) by sacrificing four infected and two control animals at fixed days post infection, as follow, B: 3, 7, 15, 30, 59, 90, 120, 150 days; BG: 7, 14, 30, 44, 62, 76, 90, 120 days; BT: 5, 8, 15, 31, 47, 61, 91, 120 days; BTG 7, 14, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 120 days.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: Shedding was assessed once a week for B single infection and 2 (BT) or 3 (BG and BTG) times a week for the co-infected rabbits.
source: Shedding was assessed once a week for B single infection and 2 (BT) or 3 (BG and BTG) times a week for the co-infected rabbits.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: Rabbits were allowed to interact with the petri dish by direct oral-nasal contact for a maximum of 10 min.
source: At every sampling point, rabbits were allowed to interact with the petri dish by direct oral-nasal contact and for a maximum of 10 min.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: Plates were incubated at 37 °C for 48 hr and colonies counted and scaled to the interaction time (CFU/s).
source: Plates were then incubated at 37 °C for 48 hr and colonies counted and scaled to the interaction time (CFU/s).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: Blood was collected once a week for neutrophils and twice a week for antibodies.
source: Briefly, for every rabbit blood was collected once a week for neutrophils and twice a week for antibodies.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: Neutrophil concentration was measured using whole blood stored in EDTA and analyzed using Hemavet-3 hematology system.
source: Neutrophil concentration was measured using whole blood (0.2 ml) stored in EDTA (Sartorius, Germany) and analyzed using Hemavet-3 hematology system (Drew Scientific, USA).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: Species-specific IgA and IgG were estimated from blood serum using B. bronchiseptica as a source of antigen and ELISA.
source: Species-specific IgA and IgG were estimated from blood serum using B. bronchiseptica as a source of antigen and ELISA (Pathak et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the experimental protocol.

claim: The model assumes that bacterial neutralization occurs through the additive effect of neutrophils, IgA, and IgG.
source: Similarly, bacterial neutralization occurs through the additive effect of these three immune variables.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated explicitly.

claim: The model assumes that the two helminths affect B. bronchiseptica infection by altering the magnitude and time course of neutrophil, IgA and IgG responses.
source: To reduce model complexity we assumed that the two helminths affect B. bronchiseptica infection, and thus shedding, by altering the magnitude and time course of neutrophil, IgA and IgG responses.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated explicitly.

claim: Model fitting was performed using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithm implemented in Stan package version 2.18.0.
source: Model fitting, and the generation of posterior distributions for the parameters estimated, was performed using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithm implemented in Stan package version 2.18.0.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the computational approach.

claim: The full model (neutrophils, IgA and IgG) was statistically better in capturing the dynamics of B. bronchiseptica shedding than the reduced formulations.
source: Results showed that the full model was statistically better in capturing the dynamics of B. bronchiseptica shedding, than the reduced formulations (Appendix 5).
evidence: This is based on model selection analysis using BIC.
